newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac pledges drive for computers, jobs for young.
newsitem.headline: Chirac pledges drive for computers, jobs for young.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac got low marks from opposition parties on Tuesday for a drive to equip schools with computers, eradicate illiteracy and encourage firms to hire young people hard hit by unemployment.
In a two-hour television interview on Monday night, Chirac also pledged better adult re-training to help people switch careers in an era when computers were rapidly gaining importance.

"A great nation is one that knows how to integrate all its children," he told France 2 television in the broadcast that echoed a drive by U.S. President Bill Clinton to computerise U.S. schools and combat illiteracy.

Politicians in the ruling centre-right coalition, gearing up for National Assembly elections in a year's time, applauded Chirac's efforts to reassure young people, hit by a 25 percent unemployment rate which is double the national average.
But the opposition Socialist party denounced what it called the "poverty of the presidential proposals".

"Young people expected concrete decisions from the president about jobs and integration, they only got a hopeless chat about questions that concern them without the slightest concrete response," said Daniel Vaillant, the Socialists' number two.
The far right National Front party also dismissed Chirac's proposals as a string of truisms. The Communist daily L'Humanite said in a front-page headline: "A lot of noise for nothing".

Chirac, speaking from Paris's Science City against a backdrop of a gleaming geodesic dome, said he wanted all secondary schools to be connected to the Internet by the year 2000 to develop computer skills and improve job prospects linked to information technology.
He also said that he wanted to eradicate illiteracy for children entering high school by the end of his seven-year mandate in the year 2002.

Chirac said that France, contrary to widespread belief, was not behind its Western partners in computers, saying it had been ahead of others in developing the Minitel telephone-based information network in the 1980s.
He said a new leap was now needed.
Chirac also said he had asked the government to cut value added tax on multimedia products and services, including CD-ROMs, to the lowest rate of 5.6 percent from 20.6 percent.

In contrast to the last major television interview he gave in December, in which he blamed the French people's innate conservatism for economic stagnation, Chirac sought to project optimism about France's dynamism.
He said, for instance, that a British factory manager who ran plants in several countries and employed 1,500 people in France had told him French workers were "by far the best".
Chirac also urged companies to do more to hire young people, accusing them of focusing too narrowly on profits.
Companies should realise that the social charges they paid rose when unemployment was high. "It's in your interest to manage your affairs so that there aren't too many social charges," he said.
Chirac again faulted French carmaker Renault for its decision announced last week to close a car factory in Belgium and lay off 3,100 workers. "I do not approve," he said.
The opposition Socialists have criticised the centre-right government for failing to head off the closure. They have trumpeted their plan to find work for 700,000 young people if elected.

An opinion poll published by the Journal du Dimanche newspaper showed young people had more confidence in themselves (65 percent) or their parents (40 percent) than in the president (13 percent) to "prepare their future and that of our society".
